chunk_findings.detail: For JSON-encoded values like the test’s own `item["new"]`, the string branch treats one redacted segment as a wildcard across the whole serialized form. Given `{"id": "knob_added:a.b", "new": '["[REDACTED:path]", "/etc/passwd"]'}` and `{"knob_added:a.b": ['["[REDACTED:path]"]']}`, `_same_value` returns `True`: `_MARK.split('["[REDACTED:path]"]')` becomes `['["', '"]']`, and the resulting regex fullmatches both one-element and two-element JSON lists because `.+?` can consume the extra `", "/etc/passwd"` part. `_unsettled` then drops the item instead of reporting it as unsettled, so a configuration change from one path to multiple paths is never planned.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_plan.py:_same_value

chunk_findings.detail: A redacted record for a one-element default like `{"knob_added:approvals.transcript_dirs": ['["[REDACTED:path]"]']}` matches *any* manifest `new` that is a one-element JSON list containing one quote-free string. For example, if the settled log redacted `["[REDACTED:path]"]` and the unreleased fragment later changes the default to `["/etc/passwd"]`, `_same_value('["/etc/passwd"]', '["[REDACTED:path]"]')` returns `True`; `_unsettled` then returns `[]` and the changed item is silently left out of the plan. The added test checks only that adding a second element is still news; it does not cover a different one-element value, so this regression would pass while real value changes are no longer applied.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_plan.py:_same_value

chunk_findings.detail: The fix still has the false-settled bug from the previous HIGH, and the added regression test should fail on it. The log redacts both `["[REDACTED:path]"]` and `["/etc/passwd"]` to the same literal placeholder such as `["[REDACTED:path]"]`. In `_unsettled`, for an item `{"id": "knob_added:approvals.transcript_dirs", "new": ["/etc/passwd"]}` whose settled record is `{"knob_added:approvals.transcript_dirs": [["[REDACTED:path]"]]}`, `_recorded_form(log, ["/etc/passwd"]) in seen` is `True`, so the changed default is treated as already settled and is omitted from `config`. The new test explicitly asserts that this changed-default case is `!= []`, so the code under review does not pass its own regression test.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_plan.py:_recorded_form/_unsettled

chunk_findings.detail: The legacy-redaction fallback still has the prior false-settled bug. `_recorded_form(log, new)` is not an exact comparison: the log redaction for a `path` text field replaces any path with the same literal placeholder, e.g. both `["[REDACTED:path]"]` and `["/etc/passwd"]` become `["[REDACTED:path]"]`. If `settled["knob_added:approvals.transcript_dirs"]` contains the legacy redacted record `["[REDACTED:path]"]`, then a plan item whose `new` is actually `["/etc/passwd"]` satisfies `_recorded_form(log, new) in seen` and is incorrectly `done`, so a changed default is treated as settled and silently dropped. The new digest only protects newly written records; it does not make old redacted records distinguishable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_plan.py:_unsettled

chunk_findings.detail: The added regression test does not answer the previous HIGH. Its `seen` record is constructed with only a digest string, `[f"{DIGEST}{dirs[0]['digest']}"]`, so it never contains the colliding redacted form `[["[REDACTED:path]"]]` that the previous finding says `_recorded_form(log, ["/etc/passwd"])` matches. An `_unsettled` implementation that still treats `_recorded_form(log, item["new"]) in seen` as settled will pass all three new assertions — the changed paths have no digest match and the colliding redacted form is absent from this `seen` — while still false-settling a real item such as `{"id": "knob_added:approvals.transcript_dirs", "new": ["/etc/passwd"]}` against a settled `[REDACTED:path]` record. This probe therefore does not protect the false-settled case from the prior HIGH.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_upgrade_apply.py:test_a_value_the_log_redacted_still_counts_as_settled

chunk_findings.detail: The new `done` only accepts a `digest:` marker in `seen` and ignores legacy pre-digest records whose stored value is an exact, non-redacted value. Given an old applied event with `config_changes=[{"change": "knob_changed", "key": "feature.flag", "old": False, "new": True}]`, the settled map contains `{"knob_changed:feature.flag": [True]}`. For the current item with `i["new"] == True`, `not seen` is false and `f"digest:{of_obj(True)}" in [True]` is false, so `_unsettled` returns this already-applied item and the plan reapplies it. This directly conflicts with `test_items_settled_by_a_partial_apply_stay_settled_when_a_newer_ddflow_is_installed`: an older partial apply without digest does not get to stay settled just because its value was not redacted. The `else c.get("new")` branch in the `news` comprehension is therefore ineffective for `_unsettled`, causing non-redacted legacy partial applies to regress.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_plan.py:_unsettled

chunk_findings.detail: `_unsettled` stores raw config values and digest markers in the same `seen` list and checks `new in seen` before the digest check. A raw value that is a string exactly equal to a digest marker of a *different* value is wrongly treated as settled. Example: a partial apply with `new="secret"` and `digest="abc"` for item `knob_set:x` makes `seen == ["digest:abc"]`; later the same item's desired value is the literal string `"digest:abc"`; `new in seen` is `True`, so the item is dropped even though the earlier partial apply wrote `"secret"`, not the literal string.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_plan.py:_unsettled

chunk_findings.detail: The new docstring says a pre-digest masked record “settles no value,” but the code does still settle one value: the mask string itself. `_settled` stores `c.get("new")` when `digest` is absent, and here `done()` does `new in seen` before any notion of “this was a redaction mask.” Concrete input: a previous partial apply of `"[REDACTED:path]"` was persisted pre-digest as `"[REDACTED:path]"`; later the same `change:key` item has desired `new == "[REDACTED:path]"` (a valid literal path). Then `seen == ["[REDACTED:path]"]`, so `new in seen` is `True` and the item is dropped without being applied, even though the old record was for a different value. This false settled case contradicts the stated behavior and can skip a real config change.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_plan.py:_unsettled

chunk_findings.detail: The redaction detection is `"[REDACTED" not in json.dumps(v)` for every verbatim pre-digest value `v == new`. This misclassifies a legitimate pre-digest record whose value merely contains a double quote immediately followed by `[REDACTED` as a log-redacted mask. For example, an older partial apply recorded `new = 'say "[REDACTED" now'` for item id `x`, and the current desired item has the same `new`. `done()` sees `v == new`, but `json.dumps(v)` contains `"[REDACTED"`, so it returns `False`; `_unsettled` then includes an already-settled item and an upgrade apply runs it again, even though the pre-digest record actually held the value verbatim and should have counted as settled according to the new docstring.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_plan.py:_unsettled

chunk_findings.detail: The new `done()` ignores pre-digest `settled` entries that contain the exact, unredacted `new` value. For an older `UPGRADE_APPLIED` record without a `digest` field, `_settled` still stores `c.get("new")` (e.g. `"[REDACTED:path]"`), but `_unsettled` now only accepts `(DIGEST, of_obj(new)) in seen`. Given `settled = {"knob_changed:x": ["[REDACTED:path]"]}` and an item `{"id": "knob_changed:x", "new": "[REDACTED:path]"}`, the item is returned as unsettled because the list has no digest tuple. That is wrong: an acknowledged pre-digest change with an unredacted recorded value is still settled, and the user is forced to re-apply it.

chunk_findings.detail: The new test only exercises a true redacted pre-digest record (`[["[REDACTED:path]"]]`) and digest-style records; it does not construct the earlier false-positive input `new = 'say "[REDACTED" now'` where the legacy value equals the current desired value but `json.dumps(v)` still contains `"[REDACTED"`. That branch still treats this legitimate value as a log-redacted mask and leaves the item unsettled, so the previous LOW finding remains unanswered by this regression test.
